h1: Diagnosing a sudden fall in brewpub beer sales with an outside review
title: Diagnosing a Fall in Brewpub Sales | Craft Beer School
desc: How an outside review diagnoses a sudden fall in brewpub beer sales: separating beer quality, service, price, season and competition with data.
teaser: Beer sales dropped by a fifth in two months and everyone has a theory. An outside review swaps theories for evidence.
standfirst: When brewpub beer sales fall suddenly, owners tend to blame the obvious: the economy, the weather, a new place down the road. Sometimes they are right. Often the cause is closer to home. A structured review finds it faster than arguments in the office.
sections:
A fall in beer sales triggers a familiar meeting. The owner blames the new venue nearby. The manager blames the price rise. The brewer blames the bar for poor service. The bar blames the brewer for the new IPA. Everyone is partly right. Nobody has the numbers to prove it.

An outside review separates the possible causes and checks each one against data, tasting and observation. It does not take sides. It looks at what changed and when.

Pull sales data from your POS for the last six to twelve months, by beer, by day and by hour. Our guide to weekly numbers for brewpub owners lists the figures worth tracking. Then ask:

  • Did the fall start on a specific date or creep in gradually?
  • Is it every beer or particular beers?
  • Is it every day or certain days and hours?
  • Did food sales fall at the same time, or only beer?
  • Did footfall fall, or are the same number of guests drinking less beer?

The answers narrow the field fast. If footfall is steady and beer sales per guest fell, the problem is inside the brewpub. If footfall fell across beer and food, the problem may be outside, or it may be the experience as a whole.
Check the beer at the tap

Taste every beer on tap as a guest would, from the glass at the bar. Then taste the same beer straight from the serving tank or keg. If the tap sample is worse, the problem is in dispense. Dirty lines give buttery or sour notes, wrong gas pressure gives flat or foamy beer and warm lines spoil the first pours of every shift. Our guide to draught line cleaning covers the routine.

If the tank sample is also off, look at recent brews. A change of malt lot, a new yeast generation, a hot fortnight in the cellar or a new brewer can all shift a beer enough for regulars to notice before staff do.

Run the check with fresh eyes. Pour each beer at the start of a shift and again at the busiest hour. The first pour after a quiet morning often comes from line beer that has warmed, which is exactly the glass a lunchtime regular gets. Check the cellar or cold room temperature too, plus the gas pressure on each keg or serving tank against the setting for that beer's carbonation. Small dispense faults rarely show up in the brewery but show up in every glass on the floor.

Ask regulars, gently, what changed for them. A few short conversations at the bar can confirm in a week what the data only hints at.

Spend a few busy evenings watching how beer is sold. Do servers recommend house beers or default to cocktails and imported bottles? Do they know what each beer tastes like? Are tasters offered? Is the tap list board current, or does it list beers that ran out a week ago?

Then look at pour quality and waste. Glassware that is not beer-clean kills head and makes good beer look flat. A high pour loss means you are selling less beer than you brew and possibly overpouring to regulars.

Check what changed on the menu and price list in the months before the fall. A price rise, a smaller glass, a removed happy hour or a rotated tap list can all hit sales. Compare the timing carefully with the data.

Season matters in India. Monsoon, exam months and festival periods change footfall and drinking patterns. Compare with the same months last year before blaming anything new. And yes, check the competition. A new venue with a strong offer can pull regulars away, but the data should show a fall in footfall that lines up with its opening.

A good review ends with a short ranked list of causes, each with the evidence behind it and a plan for each. That might be a line cleaning schedule and staff tasting session, a recipe correction, a tap list rethink using sales data or a price adjustment. It should also set the numbers to watch over the next eight weeks to see whether the fix is working.

If sales have been sliding for a long time and the problems are tangled, our guide to turning around a struggling brewpub covers the broader recovery.
faqs: How quickly can an outside review find the cause of falling sales?
With POS data, a few evenings of observation and a full tasting, the main causes usually become clear within a couple of weeks. Confirming the fix takes longer.
Could the problem be the beer even if we have not changed the recipe?
Yes. Malt lots, yeast generations, cellar temperatures and dirty draught lines can all change a beer without any recipe change. Taste from tank and tap side by side.
What data do we need for a sales review?
Sales by beer, day and hour for six to twelve months, footfall or covers, menu and price change dates, brew records and any staff changes.
